technique.how: Curvilinear or phased-array probe, patient supine: RUQ (hepatorenal/Morison's pouch, sweep to caudal liver tip and right paracolic gutter), LUQ (splenorenal and subphrenic spaces), pelvis (rectovesical/rectouterine pouch, transverse and sagittal, ideally with filled bladder), plus subxiphoid cardiac view. An anechoic stripe in a dependent space = free fluid.
technique.prerequisites: Trained operator; full bladder improves the pelvic view; repeat the exam if the first is negative and suspicion persists.
technique.contraindications: None; do not delay laparotomy in an unstable patient with a clear indication.

interpretation.positive_finding: Free fluid in a hypotensive blunt-trauma patient is hemoperitoneum until proven otherwise (adjusted summary LR+ 30) and sends the patient to laparotomy or CT depending on stability. In non-trauma patients it shows ascites/free fluid but not its nature.
interpretation.negative_finding: A negative FAST lowers but does not exclude intra-abdominal injury (adjusted LR− 0.26; pooled sensitivity 74–82%). It does not exclude retroperitoneal, hollow-viscus or solid-organ injury without hemoperitoneum.
interpretation.pitfalls: Needs roughly 200+ mL to be visible; pre-existing ascites, ovarian cysts, bladder, perinephric fat and pericolic fluid mimic blood. Obesity, bowel gas and subcutaneous emphysema limit windows, and all pooled estimates are trauma-only.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive in unstable trauma → OR; positive in stable → CT; negative with persistent suspicion → CT or serial FAST. Non-trauma free fluid → paracentesis to characterize.

estimates.target_condition: Intra-abdominal injury after blunt abdominal trauma — abnormal bedside FAST (intraperitoneal fluid or organ injury); random-effects bivariate summary, unadjusted for publication bias
estimates.population: Adult ED patients with blunt abdominal trauma; 22 bedside ultrasonography studies (evidence levels 1–3)
estimates.reference_standard: Abdominal CT, diagnostic peritoneal lavage, laparotomy, autopsy and/or clinical course
estimates.quote: Abnormal FAST examination result, bedside (all US references) Unadjusted 82 (75–89) 99 (98–99) 69 (38–101) 0.18 (0.11–0.25)

estimates.target_condition: Intra-abdominal injury after blunt abdominal trauma — abnormal bedside FAST; random-effects univariate summary adjusted for publication bias
estimates.population: Adult ED patients with blunt abdominal trauma; 22 bedside ultrasonography studies (evidence levels 1–3)
estimates.reference_standard: Abdominal CT, diagnostic peritoneal lavage, laparotomy, autopsy and/or clinical course

sources.citation: Nishijima DK, Simel DL, Wisner DH, Holmes JF. Does this adult patient have a blunt intra-abdominal injury? JAMA 2012.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Not validated for non-trauma hypotension or for characterizing fluid; do not use a negative FAST to stop work-up in penetrating trauma or suspected hollow-viscus injury.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Positive FAST with hypotension after trauma is a surgical emergency — activate trauma surgery and massive transfusion.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Accuracy varied across the 22 included studies (individual results in eTable 3, not accessible); no pooled interobserver statistic reported.
safety_scope.skill_assumption: Operator credentialed in FAST/eFAST; pooled estimates come from emergency physicians, surgeons and radiologists in trauma centres, not novices.

extraction_notes: RCE anchor PMID 22496266 confirmed; PMC4966670 open-access body text read. Both Table 4 FAST rows entered as separate estimates (unadjusted bivariate vs publication-bias-adjusted univariate) rather than averaged; the adjusted row is the more conservative planning number. Prevalence quote: "The prevalence of intra-abdominal injury in adult emergency department patients with blunt abdominal trauma among all evidence level 1 and 2 studies was 13% (95% CI, 10%-17%)" (Abstract, Results). Reference standard as stated in the abstract. Table 4 does not state a fluid-volume threshold; index test is 'abnormal FAST' (free fluid or organ injury), so estimates are for the FAST result rather than 'free fluid' alone — a minor mismatch with the id title. All data are trauma-only; no diagnostic-accuracy data for FAST-view free fluid in cirrhosis/SBP, AAA rupture or perforated viscus were sought within budget, so those differentials remain unquantified.
